\part*{Chapter 2 --- Basic Theorems}
\addcontentsline{toc}{part}{Chapter 2 --- Basic Theorems}
This chapter covers all 96 numbered problems in Sections 7--12 (printed pp.~89--151), including the starred problems. The identifiers continue the textbook's numbering. Smooth means $C^\infty$ when no finite differentiability class is specified. Perturbation remainders are uniform on fixed compact time intervals, unless a longer interval is explicitly justified.

\Needspace{14\baselineskip}
\section{Rectification theorems (\texorpdfstring{$\S7$}{Section 7})}
\prob{7.1/1}{Two local straightening maps}{90}
Retain $t$ as the first coordinate. For $\dot x=t$, put $y=x-t^2/2$; then $\dot y=0$ and the inverse is $x=y+t^2/2$. For $\dot x=x^2$, put
\[
 y=\frac{x}{1+tx},\qquad x=\frac{y}{1-ty}.
\]
Near $(0,0)$ the denominators are nonzero, $y_x=(1+tx)^{-2}$, and $y_t+x^2y_x=0$. These are local diffeomorphisms carrying integral curves to horizontal lines.

\prob{7.1/2}{Global straightening can fail}{90}
No. In fact the smooth everywhere nonvertical example in Problem 7.1/4 below already supplies a counterexample on the plane. Its space of maximal leaves is not Hausdorff, whereas the leaves of the horizontal foliation of the whole plane are parametrized by a real coordinate and have Hausdorff leaf space. A global diffeomorphism onto the plane cannot change this property. Here and in 7.1/4, global straightening means straightening on the whole space onto the whole space; a coordinate chart onto a proper open set is a different requirement.

\prob{7.1/3}{A plane field that cannot be straightened}{90}
On $\R^3$ consider the planes $\ker(dz+y\,dx)$. Their projection to the $(x,y)$-plane is an isomorphism at every point. A surface tangent to these planes would therefore locally be a graph $z=f(x,y)$, with
\[
 f_x=-y,\qquad f_y=0.
\]
The second equation makes $f$ independent of $y$, contradicting the first. Thus there are no local integral surfaces. A field of parallel planes has integral surfaces, and their inverse images under a straightening diffeomorphism would give the impossible surfaces above. Equivalently, $(dz+y\,dx)\wedge d(dz+y\,dx)$ is nowhere zero.

\prob{7.1/4*}{An everywhere nonvertical global counterexample}{91}
Consider $\dot x=tx^2$ on the entire $(t,x)$-plane. Its nonzero solutions satisfy
\[
 \frac1x=C-\frac{t^2}{2}.
\]
For $C<0$ this is one complete negative solution. At $C=0$ there are two different maximal leaves $L_-$ and $L_+$, given by $x=-2/t^2$ for $t<0$ and $t>0$, respectively. They are not one leaf: neither extends through $t=0$.

No disjoint saturated open sets can contain $L_-$ and $L_+$. Indeed, the points on the $C<0$ leaves at $t=-1$ and $t=1$ tend to $(-1,-2)$ and $(1,-2)$ as $C\uparrow0$. Any such two open sets therefore both meet the same leaf for $C$ sufficiently close to zero; saturation makes them intersect. Thus the leaf space is not Hausdorff, ruling out a diffeomorphism to the horizontal foliation of the whole plane. Taking extra constant dependent variables gives the same obstruction in higher dimension. This example also shows why local existence alone does not provide global straightening.

\prob{7.1/5}{Straightening without changing time}{91}
Fix $(t_0,a_0)$ and let $\Phi(t;t_0,a)$ be the local solution with initial value $a$. The map
\[
 (t,a)\longmapsto(t,\Phi(t;t_0,a))
\]
has invertible derivative at $(t_0,a_0)$ because $D_a\Phi(t_0;t_0,a_0)=I$. Its local inverse has the form $(t,x)\mapsto(t,y(t,x))$. Along a solution $y$ is precisely its initial value at $t_0$, hence $\dot y=0$. The inverse function theorem therefore gives the required time-preserving local straightening.

\prob{7.1/6}{A global time-preserving example}{91}
For $\dot x=x+t$, set $y=e^{-t}(x+t+1)$. Direct differentiation gives $\dot y=0$. The inverse $x=e^ty-t-1$ exists for every $(t,y)\in\R^2$, so this is a global time-preserving diffeomorphism.

\prob{7.1/7}{Why the Riccati equation cannot be globally straightened with time fixed}{91}
For $\dot x=x^2$, the nonzero solution $x(t)=a/(1-at)$ has a finite endpoint of its maximal time interval. A time-preserving diffeomorphism of the entire plane taking this equation to $\dot y=0$ would have an inverse defined along the entire horizontal line $y=y_0$, producing a solution for every $t\in\R$. This contradicts the finite-time blow-up. The local transformation in 7.1/1 is not defined globally.

\prob{7.1/8}{Newton's series for the exponential}{91}
Write $x=\sum_{j\ge0}a_jt^j$ in $\dot x=x$, $x(0)=1$. Comparing coefficients gives $a_0=1$ and $(j+1)a_{j+1}=a_j$, hence $a_j=1/j!$. The ratio test proves convergence for every real or complex $t$, and uniform convergence on compact sets justifies termwise differentiation. The resulting solution is $x=e^t$.

\prob{7.3/1}{Variation of a scalar initial condition}{94}
For $\dot x=x^2+x\sin t$, $x(0)=a$, the solution at $a=0$ is zero. Its derivative $z=\partial_a x|_{a=0}$ solves $\dot z=(\sin t)z$, $z(0)=1$. Thus
\[
 \boxed{z(t)=e^{1-\cos t}},\qquad x(t;a)=a e^{1-\cos t}+O(a^2).
\]
The error statement is on each fixed compact interval, for sufficiently small $a$.

\prob{7.3/2}{A perturbed Lotka--Volterra phase curve}{94}
For $\dot x=x(1-ya(x,y))$, $\dot y=y(x-1)$, divide by $\dot x$ near $(1,0)$:
\[
 \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{y(x-1)}{x(1-ya(x,y))},\qquad y(1)=\varepsilon.
\]
Set $y=\varepsilon z+O(\varepsilon^2)$. Then $z'=(1-1/x)z$, $z(1)=1$, so
\[
 \boxed{y(x)=\varepsilon\frac{e^{x-1}}x+O(\varepsilon^2)}.
\]
The estimate holds on compact intervals of $x>0$ where this perturbative branch is defined. It describes the portion near the $x$-axis, not an entire closed orbit.

\prob{7.3/3}{Initial-angle derivative of the pendulum}{94}
For $\ddot\theta=-\sin\theta$, $\theta(0)=a$, $\dot\theta(0)=0$, differentiation at $a=0$ gives $\ddot z=-z$, $z(0)=1$, $\dot z(0)=0$. Consequently $z=\cos t$ and $\partial_a\dot\theta|_0=-\sin t$. Uniqueness and the odd symmetry of the equation imply $\theta(t;-a)=-\theta(t;a)$; smooth dependence therefore improves the fixed-time expansion to $\theta=a\cos t+O(a^3)$. This does not bound the error uniformly for arbitrarily large time.

\prob{7.3/4}{The first variation of a soft oscillator}{95}
For $\ddot x=-x^3$, $x(0)=0$, $\dot x(0)=a$, the first variation satisfies $\ddot z=0$, $z(0)=0$, $\dot z(0)=1$. Thus $x=at+O(a^3)$ on fixed time intervals. Substituting an odd expansion gives more precisely
\[
 x(t;a)=at-\frac{a^3t^5}{20}+O(a^5)
\]
on such intervals: the cubic coefficient has second derivative $-t^3$ and zero initial data.

\prob{7.3/5}{The time scale on which the relative error is small}{95}
Let $X''=-X^3$, $X(0)=0$, $X'(0)=1$. For $a\ne0$, uniqueness and scaling give exactly
\[
 x(t;a)=\operatorname{sgn}(a)\sqrt{|a|}\,X(\sqrt{|a|}t).
\]
Near zero, $X(s)=s-s^5/20+O(s^9)$. Hence, interpreting the quotient at $t=0$ by continuity,
\[
 \frac{x(t;a)-at}{at}=-\frac{|a|^2t^4}{20}+O(|a|^4t^8).
\]
This tends to zero whenever $\sqrt{|a|}|t|\to0$, proving the requested regime $|t|\ll |a|^{-1/2}$, including intervals whose lengths grow as $a\to0$. Energy gives amplitude $2^{1/4}\sqrt{|a|}$, consistent with this scale.

\prob{7.4/1}{The period map and the order of composition}{97}
Write $G(t,s)$ for the evolution map and $A=G(T,0)$. Periodicity and uniqueness give $G(t+T,s+T)=G(t,s)$; the evolution law gives $G(t,s)G(s,r)=G(t,r)$. Since all maps are globally defined and invertible, these imply $G(kT,0)=A^k$ for every integer $k$. Moreover
\[
 G(kT+s,0)=G(kT+s,kT)G(kT,0)=G(s,0)A^k.
\]
Thus the second displayed ordering in the book is the valid one. There is no general reason for $A$ to commute with $G(s,0)$.

\prob{7.5/1}{A parameter derivative of the logistic solution}{98}
For $\dot x=x(a-x)$, $x(0)=1$, the base solution at $a=1$ is $x=1$. Differentiating with respect to $a$ yields $\dot z=1-z$, $z(0)=0$. Therefore $\partial_a x(t;1)=1-e^{-t}$.

\prob{7.5/2}{A small constant torque}{99}
For $\ddot\theta=a-\sin\theta$ with zero initial angle and velocity, the derivative at $a=0$ obeys $\ddot z=1-z$, $z(0)=\dot z(0)=0$. It is $z=1-\cos t$. Hence $\theta=a(1-\cos t)+O(a^2)$ on each fixed finite interval (odd symmetry in fact gives $O(a^3)$).

\prob{7.5/3}{Varying an oscillator's frequency}{99}
The solution is $\theta(t;\omega)=\cos(\omega t)$, so $\partial_\omega\theta|_{\omega=1}=-t\sin t$. Thus $\theta(t;1+\varepsilon)=\cos t-\varepsilon t\sin t+O(\varepsilon^2t^2)$ by Taylor's theorem. The growing first-order term is a phase error, not an unbounded exact oscillation. A small phase error requires $|\varepsilon t|\ll1$.

\prob{7.6/1}{A compact set need not be exited by an arbitrary direction field}{101}
Take the nonzero field $(y,-x)$ on the punctured plane and the compact annulus $1\le x^2+y^2\le2$. A circle of radius strictly between $1$ and $\sqrt2$ stays in the interior forever and never meets the boundary. The extension-to-boundary assertion in extended phase space uses the strictly increasing time coordinate; it does not hold for an arbitrary direction field.

\prob{7.6/2}{Linear growth prevents finite-time escape}{101}
Fix a finite time window $|t-t_0|\le T$. Smoothness on its product with $|x|\le r$ gives a bound $M_T$ there. Together with the assumed estimate outside the ball, this gives $|v(t,x)|\le M_T+k|x|$ everywhere in this window. The integral equation and Gronwall's inequality give, for both forward and backward time,
\[
 |x(t)|\le (|x(t_0)|+M_T|t-t_0|)e^{k|t-t_0|}.
\]
Thus the graph stays in a compact subset of the full domain on every finite time interval. The extension theorem excludes a finite maximal endpoint, proving completeness in both directions. No bound uniform in all time on the interior ball is needed.

\prob{7.6/3}{Complete solutions define a flow}{103}
Put $g^t(x)=\Phi(t;0,x)$. Completeness defines this for all $(t,x)$. Uniqueness gives $g^0=\mathrm{id}$ and $g^{s+t}=g^s\circ g^t$. In particular $g^{-t}$ is the inverse of $g^t$. Local smooth dependence, applied along any finite orbit segment and composed over finitely many subintervals, makes $(t,x)\mapsto g^t(x)$ smooth. These maps are therefore a global phase flow.

\prob{7.7/1}{Straightening the oscillator's vector field}{104}
Near $(x_1,x_2)=(1,0)$ use $x_1=r\cos\theta$, $x_2=-r\sin\theta$, with the local branch of $\theta$ near zero. For $\dot x_1=x_2$, $\dot x_2=-x_1$, direct differentiation gives $\dot r=0$, $\dot\theta=1$. Thus the vector field becomes $\partial_\theta$, with its speed as well as its direction straightened.

\prob{7.7/2}{Three explicit vector-field rectifications}{104}
In each case the new coordinates $(s,z)$ satisfy $\dot s=1$, $\dot z=0$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item For $x_1\partial_{x_1}+2x_2\partial_{x_2}$ on $x_1>0$, choose $s=\log x_1$, $z=x_2/x_1^2$. The inverse is $(x_1,x_2)=(e^s,ze^{2s})$.
\item For $\partial_{x_1}+\sin x_1\partial_{x_2}$, choose $s=x_1$, $z=x_2+\cos x_1$. The inverse is $(s,z-\cos s)$.
\item For $x_1\partial_{x_1}+(1-x_1^2)\partial_{x_2}$ on $|x_1|<1$, choose $s=x_2+x_1^2/2$, $z=x_1e^{-s}$. Then $\dot s=1$ and $\dot z=0$, including at $x_1=0$. The inverse is $x_1=ze^s$, $x_2=s-z^2e^{2s}/2$, with image domain $|z|e^s<1$.
\end{enumerate}

\Needspace{14\baselineskip}
\section{Higher-order equations (\texorpdfstring{$\S8$}{Section 8})}
\prob{8.1/1}{The second finite difference}{106}
For $\Delta_h\varphi(t)=\varphi(t+h)-\varphi(t)$, apply the same operator once more:
\[
 \Delta_h^2\varphi(t)=[\varphi(t+2h)-\varphi(t+h)]-[\varphi(t+h)-\varphi(t)]
 =\varphi(t+2h)-2\varphi(t+h)+\varphi(t).
\]

\prob{8.1/2}{Vanishing differences and polynomial sequences}{106}
Fix $t$ and write $a_k=\varphi(t+kh)$. If $a_k$ is a polynomial in $k$ of degree less than $n$, each forward difference reduces its degree, so $\Delta^n a=0$. Conversely, define
\[
 P(k)=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\binom{k}{j}(\Delta^j a)_0,
 \qquad \binom{k}{j}=\frac{k(k-1)\cdots(k-j+1)}{j!}.
\]
Since $\Delta\binom{k}{j}=\binom{k}{j-1}$, this polynomial has the prescribed first $n$ difference data. Thus $a-P$ has its first $n$ values zero and satisfies $\Delta^n(a-P)=0$. The recurrence
$\sum_{j=0}^n(-1)^{n-j}\binom nj(a-P)_{k+j}=0$
determines values uniquely both forwards and backwards. Hence $a_k=P(k)$ for every integer $k$.
\review{The assertion is on each lattice $t+h\mathbb Z$. It does not say $\varphi$ is a polynomial as a function on $\R$: an $h$-periodic function already has $\Delta_h\varphi=0$.}

\prob{8.1/3}{Vanishing ordinary derivatives}{107}
Repeated integration of $x^{(n)}=0$ yields
\[
 x(t)=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac{x^{(j)}(t_0)}{j!}(t-t_0)^j
\]
on the connected interval of definition. Conversely the $n$th derivative of each such polynomial is zero. The constants are arbitrary, giving an $n$-dimensional solution space.

\prob{8.1/4}{Radial solutions of the planar Helmholtz equation}{107}
For $u(x,y)=f(r)$, $r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}>0$, direct differentiation gives $\Delta u=f''+f'/r$. Hence $\Delta u+u=0$ becomes
\[
 f''(r)+\frac1r f'(r)+f(r)=0.
\]
It is a smooth linear second-order equation on $(0,\infty)$. The values $f(r_0),f'(r_0)$ at any $r_0>0$ determine a unique solution on that interval. Thus the radial solution space has dimension two. Requiring smooth extension through $r=0$, which the problem excludes, would impose an additional restriction.

\prob{8.2/1}{An equation admitting both the sine and the identity}{107}
At $t=0$, $t$ and $\sin t$ have the same derivatives of orders zero, one, and two, but they are different functions. Uniqueness for a smooth equation solved for its highest derivative rules out orders $n\le3$ on a domain containing these initial data. Every $n\ge4$ is possible: both solve $x^{(n)}+x^{(n-2)}=0$. The information therefore gives $n\ge4$, not one uniquely determined order.

\prob{8.2/2}{The impossible configuration in Figure 77}{108}
For $\ddot x+p(t)\dot x+q(t)x=0$, every scalar multiple $c\varphi_1$ is also a solution. The configuration in the figure forces a multiple $c\varphi_1$ to be tangent to $\varphi_2$ at an interior point while the two curves do not coincide. One way to see the tangency is to take an interior extremum of $\varphi_2/\varphi_1$ in the depicted positive region. At this point both values and first derivatives of $c\varphi_1$ and $\varphi_2$ agree. Second-order uniqueness makes the solutions identical, a contradiction.

\prob{8.2/3}{Why a singular equation loses uniqueness}{108}
Both $x=0$ and $x=t^2$ satisfy $t^2\ddot x=2x$ and $x(0)=\dot x(0)=0$. For $t\ne0$ the normal form is $\ddot x=2x/t^2$, whose right-hand side is not defined near the initial point $t=0$. At $t=0$ the original equation does not determine $\ddot x$. The hypotheses of the normal-form uniqueness theorem are therefore absent.

\prob{8.2/4}{A quadratic sequence from difference data}{108}
With step $h=1$, $\Delta^3\varphi=0$ gives a quadratic sequence. Newton's formula from 8.1/2 gives
\[
 \varphi(k)=0+0\binom{k}{1}+2\binom{k}{2}=k(k-1),\qquad k\in\mathbb Z.
\]
Indeed $\Delta\varphi(k)=2k$ and $\Delta^2\varphi(k)=2$, so all initial conditions hold.

\prob{8.3/1}{First-order correction to a fall with weak resistance}{108}
For $\ddot x=-g+\varepsilon F(x,\dot x)$, $x(0)=h$, $\dot x(0)=0$, put $x=x_0+\varepsilon x_1+O(\varepsilon^2)$. The unperturbed fall is $x_0=h-gt^2/2$ and
\[
 x_1''(t)=F(h-gt^2/2,-gt),\qquad
 x_1(t)=\int_0^t(t-s)F(h-gs^2/2,-gs)\dd s.
\]
This is the first-order position correction for general smooth $F$. Let $T_0=\sqrt{2h/g}$. The impact time is
\[
 T_\varepsilon=T_0+\varepsilon\frac{x_1(T_0)}{gT_0}+O(\varepsilon^2),
\]
by the implicit function theorem at the simple zero of $x_0$. For linear drag $F=-\dot x$, one obtains $x_1=gt^3/6$ and the delay $T_\varepsilon-T_0=\varepsilon h/(3g)+O(\varepsilon^2)$.

\prob{8.3/2}{Completeness of the pendulum}{109}
Since $|\ddot\theta|=|\sin\theta|\le1$, for any finite $|t-t_0|\le T$ we have
\[
 |\dot\theta(t)|\le|\dot\theta(t_0)|+T,\quad
 |\theta(t)|\le|\theta(t_0)|+|\dot\theta(t_0)|T+T^2/2.
\]
The pair $(\theta,\dot\theta)$ stays bounded on finite intervals, so the extension theorem gives existence for every real time. The same conclusion holds on the cylindrical phase space.

\prob{8.3/3}{Completeness for a power-law acceleration}{109}
For positive integers $k$, all solutions of $\ddot x=x^k$ are complete precisely when $k=1$: then $x=Ae^t+Be^{-t}$. For $k>1$, set $p=2/(k-1)$ and choose $A>0$ with $A^{k-1}=p(p+1)$. The function
\[
 x(t)=A(T-t)^{-p},\qquad t<T,
\]
satisfies the equation and blows up at $T$, disproving completeness of all solutions. If the convention $0\in\mathbb N$ is used, $k=0$ must be added: $\ddot x=1$ also has only complete solutions.

\prob{8.4/1}{Eastward deflection in a mine shaft}{110}
Use unit vectors east, north, and up. At latitude $\lambda$,
$\boldsymbol\Omega=\Omega(0,\cos\lambda,\sin\lambda)$.
To first order in $\Omega$, the falling velocity is $(0,0,-gt)$, so $2\boldsymbol v\times\boldsymbol\Omega$ has east component $2g\Omega t\cos\lambda$. Integrating twice with zero initial displacement and horizontal velocity gives
\[
 d_E(t)=\frac{g\Omega\cos\lambda}{3}t^3+O(\Omega^2).
\]
At $T=\sqrt{2h/g}$ this is $d_E=\frac23\Omega hT\cos\lambda+O(\Omega^2)$. Taking $h=10\,\mathrm m$, $\lambda=60^\circ$, $g=9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ and $\Omega\simeq7.3\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ gives $d_E\simeq0.348\,\mathrm{mm}$, eastward. These are the idealized constants used for the exercise.

\prob{8.4/2}{The lens cap thrown toward the Earth}{111--112}
Use the orbital radius and inverse orbital angular speed as units. The station has $r=1$, $\varphi=t$, and the cap has initial radial velocity $-v$, with $v\ll1$. Newton's equation in polar coordinates is
\[
 \ddot r-r\dot\varphi^2=-r^{-2},\qquad r\ddot\varphi+2\dot r\dot\varphi=0.
\]
Write $r=1+\rho$, $\varphi=t+\psi$ and keep first-order terms:
\[
 \ddot\rho=3\rho+2\dot\psi,\qquad \ddot\psi+2\dot\rho=0.
\]
The initial data are $\rho=\psi=\dot\psi=0$, $\dot\rho=-v$. Thus $\dot\psi=-2\rho$, $\ddot\rho=-\rho$, and
\[
 \rho=-v\sin t,\qquad \psi=2v(1-\cos t).
\]
Relative to the station, the radial and along-track displacements trace the ellipse
\[
 \frac{\rho^2}{v^2}+\frac{(\psi-2v)^2}{4v^2}=1
\]
to first order. It initially goes Earthward, then ahead, then outward, and returns close to the station after one revolution. For the book's $v\simeq1/800$ and orbital radius $6400\,\mathrm{km}$, the semiaxes are about $8$ and $16\,\mathrm{km}$ and the maximum lead about $32\,\mathrm{km}$.

This relative ellipse is an approximation, not an exact closed orbit in the rotating frame. In the two-body model the cap's inertial orbit has energy $(-1+v^2)/2$, semimajor axis $(1-v^2)^{-1}$, and eccentricity $v$. Its period differs from $2\pi$ at order $v^2$, so exact reunion after one station revolution is not implied. The error in position on that fixed interval is $O(v^2)$ in orbital-radius units.

\prob{8.5/1}{The cubic Clairaut equation}{113}
Put $p=\dot x$ in $x=tp-p^3$. For a twice differentiable solution,
\[
 0=(t-3p^2)\dot p.
\]
On regular pieces $p=c$, giving the straight lines $x=ct-c^3$. The exceptional set is $t=3p^2$, $x=2p^3$, whose projection is the semicubical cusp $27x^2=4t^3$, $t\ge0$. Its two envelope branches are
\[
 x=\pm\frac{2}{3\sqrt3}t^{3/2},\qquad t>0,
\]
and each is a solution, with slope $p=\pm\sqrt{t/3}$. A line of slope $c$ is tangent to the envelope at $(3c^2,2c^3)$.

At a given $(t,x)$, the possible slopes are the real roots of $p^3-tp+x=0$. There are three distinct roots when $4t^3-27x^2>0$, one when it is negative, and multiple roots on the cusp. Each simple root defines a smooth normal equation locally. One must specify a branch before invoking uniqueness. In the class of $C^1$ solutions, tangent line pieces can be joined to envelope pieces at the tangency points; these joins need not be $C^2$. At the cusp the envelope itself is $C^1$ from the right but not $C^2$.

\prob{8.5/2}{Integral curves on a folded equation surface}{115}
The surface $p^2=t$ has coordinates $(p,x)$. The contact equation $dx=p\,dt$ becomes $dx=2p^2\,dp$. Consequently its lifted integral curves and their projections are
\[
 (t,x,p)=(p^2,C+2p^3/3,p),\qquad (x-C)^2=4t^3/9.
\]
For $t>0$ the two projected branches are $x=C\pm2t^{3/2}/3$. The lifted curve is smooth at $p=0$, while the projection has a cusp there and is not one single-valued solution graph across both branches.

\prob{8.5/3}{General Clairaut equations and duality}{116}
On $x=tp-f(p)$ use coordinates $(t,p)$. The contact equation reduces to $(t-f'(p))dp=0$. Away from the exceptional set $t=f'(p)$, integral curves have $p=c$ and project to $x=ct-f(c)$. The discriminant/envelope is
\[
 t=f'(c),\qquad x=cf'(c)-f(c).
\]
Where $f''(c)\ne0$, invert $t=f'(c)$ and call the resulting graph $x=g(t)$. Differentiation gives $g'(t)=c$, proving tangency of the associated line. It also gives $tg'(t)-g(t)=f(c)$, so taking the Legendre transform again recovers $f$. This proves the stated local duality. At points with $f''=0$ the inversion must be considered separately; global single-valued duality needs additional assumptions such as strict convexity.

\prob{8.5/4}{Legendre transform of a power}{116}
For $f(p)=|p|^\alpha/\alpha$, $\alpha>1$, the relation $t=f'(p)=\operatorname{sgn}(p)|p|^{\alpha-1}$ has inverse $p=\operatorname{sgn}(t)|t|^{1/(\alpha-1)}$. Therefore
\[
 tp-f(p)=\left(1-\frac1\alpha\right)|t|^{\alpha/(\alpha-1)}
 =\frac{|t|^\beta}{\beta},\qquad \frac1\alpha+\frac1\beta=1.
\]
The formula includes zero by continuity. The strictly convex supremum definition gives the same transform even when the relevant higher derivatives at zero do not exist.

\Needspace{14\baselineskip}
\section{Autonomous phase curves (\texorpdfstring{$\S9$}{Section 9})}
\prob{9.1/1}{Is the variational equation autonomous?}{117}
Along a solution $x_0(t)$ of $\dot x=v(x)$, the variational equation is $\dot z=Dv(x_0(t))z$. At an equilibrium its coefficients are constant, hence it is autonomous. Generally they vary with time: for $\dot x=x^2$ and $x_0(t)=1/(1-t)$, one gets $\dot z=2z/(1-t)$. A nonstationary base solution can still give an autonomous variational equation, for example when $v$ is linear.

\prob{9.2/1}{Unique phase curves do not imply autonomy}{118}
The nonautonomous equation $\dot x=1+t^2$ has solutions $x=t+t^3/3+C$. Each maximal solution maps $\R$ onto $\R$, so there is only one phase curve as a subset of phase space: the entire line. Yet the velocity explicitly depends on time.
\review{For an autonomous equation, the proof that intersecting maximal phase curves coincide also covers incomplete solutions. Shift the time parameter to match one common point. Uniqueness makes the shifted solutions equal on their common interval; if either interval extended beyond the other, it would extend the supposedly maximal solution. Thus their shifted intervals, and hence their images, agree.}

\prob{9.3/1}{Closed subgroups of the plane, space, and circle}{120}
Every closed additive subgroup of $\R^n$ has the form
\[
 G=V\oplus\left(\mathbb Zb_1+\cdots+\mathbb Zb_k\right),
\]
where $V$ is a vector subspace and the $b_i$ are linearly independent vectors in $V^\perp$. Thus, up to an invertible linear change of coordinates, it is $\R^p\times\mathbb Z^k\times\{0\}^{n-p-k}$, with $p+k\le n$. For $n=2$ the types are $\{0\},\mathbb Z,\mathbb Z^2,\R,\R\times\mathbb Z,\R^2$; for $n=3$ they are those six together with $\mathbb Z^3,\R\times\mathbb Z^2,\R^2\times\mathbb Z,\R^3$. Lattices need not align with the original coordinate axes.

Here is a proof of the structural assertion. If a closed subgroup contains nonzero $g_j\to0$ with $g_j/|g_j|\to e$, integer multiples of $g_j$ approximate every $se$, so it contains the line $\R e$. Let $V$ be a maximal vector subspace contained in $G$. Orthogonal projection onto $V^\perp$ identifies the remaining subgroup with $D=G\cap V^\perp$: subtracting a vector in $V$ stays in $G$. It is closed and must be discrete, since otherwise the preceding argument would enlarge $V$.

A discrete subgroup $D$ is a lattice in its linear span. To verify this by induction, choose a shortest nonzero vector $b_1$. The projection of $D$ to $b_1^\perp$ is discrete: otherwise choose projected vectors tending to zero, subtract integer multiples of $b_1$ to bound their components along $b_1$, and take a convergent subsequence. A discrete subgroup has only finitely many points in a compact set (differences of an accumulating sequence would tend to zero), giving a contradiction. Apply induction to the projected group and lift its basis. The kernel is $\mathbb Zb_1$ by the shortest-vector property, so these lifts together with $b_1$ generate $D$ freely.

Finally a closed subgroup $H\subset S^1$ has closed inverse image under $t\mapsto e^{it}$, containing $2\pi\mathbb Z$. The closed-subgroup classification of $\R$ gives either $\R$ or $(2\pi/m)\mathbb Z$ for a positive integer $m$. Hence $H=S^1$ or the group of all $m$th roots of unity, including the trivial group for $m=1$.

\prob{9.3/2}{Orbit closures of two incommensurate oscillators}{121}
For $\ddot x_1=-x_1$, $\ddot x_2=-2x_2$, the quantities $r_1^2=x_1^2+\dot x_1^2$ and $r_2^2=x_2^2+\dot x_2^2/2$ are constant. If both vanish, the orbit is a point. If just one vanishes, it is a periodic ellipse, diffeomorphic to a circle. If both are positive, the orbit lies on the product of the two ellipses, a two-torus, with angle velocities $1$ and $\sqrt2$.

It is dense in that torus. To approximate any first angle, sample times $t=\alpha+2\pi m$; the second angles then differ by $2\pi m\sqrt2$. Irrational rotation is dense: the pigeonhole principle supplies nonzero integer multiples arbitrarily close to zero modulo $1$, and their successive multiples approximate any point of the circle. Thus the orbit closure is the whole two-torus, although the orbit itself is not closed.

\Needspace{14\baselineskip}
\section{Directional derivatives and first integrals (\texorpdfstring{$\S10$}{Section 10})}
\prob{10.1/1}{The Hamiltonian differentiated along its own field}{122}
For $X_H=\sum_i(H_{p_i}\partial_{q_i}-H_{q_i}\partial_{p_i})$, the chain rule gives
\[
 L_{X_H}H=\sum_i(H_{q_i}H_{p_i}-H_{p_i}H_{q_i})=0.
\]
This is the differential form of conservation of the Hamiltonian.

\prob{10.3/1}{Which directional-derivative identities hold?}{123}
The coordinate formula $L_vf=\sum_i v_i\partial_i f$ gives additivity in $f$ and the Leibniz rule by the corresponding rules for partial derivatives. It also gives $L_{u+v}=L_u+L_v$ and $L_{fu}=fL_u$ by distributing the coefficients. The fifth identity is false in general. For $u=\partial_x$, $v=x\partial_x$, and $f=x$,
\[
 L_uL_vf=1,\qquad L_vL_uf=0.
\]
Commutation of coordinate partial derivatives does not cancel the derivatives of the variable coefficients of a field.

\prob{10.3/2*}{Every smooth derivation comes from a vector field}{124}
Yes, for derivations of the $\R$-algebra $C^\infty(U)$, hence $\R$-linear derivations. Let $D$ be such a derivation and put $v_i=D(x_i)$; these are smooth functions. First $D1=2D1$, so $D$ annihilates constants. It is local at each point $p$: if $f=0$ near $p$, choose a smooth bump $\chi$ equal to $1$ near $p$ and supported where $f=0$. From $D(\chi f)=0$ evaluated at $p$, obtain $(Df)(p)=0$.

On a small convex ball about $p$, Hadamard's formula gives
\[
 f(x)=f(p)+\sum_i(x_i-p_i)h_i(x),\qquad
 h_i(x)=\int_0^1\partial_i f(p+s(x-p))\dd s.
\]
Use cutoffs to extend the $h_i$ to $U$ without changing their germs at $p$. Locality and the product rule then give
\[
 (Df)(p)=\sum_i(Dx_i)(p)h_i(p)=\sum_i v_i(p)\partial_i f(p).
\]
Thus $D=L_v$. Uniqueness follows by applying $L_v$ to the coordinate functions. This proves that $v\mapsto L_v$ is an isomorphism of $C^\infty(U)$-modules.

\prob{10.4/1}{The commutator is first order}{124}
Expanding twice gives
\[
 (L_aL_b-L_bL_a)f
 =\sum_j\left(\sum_i a_i\partial_i b_j-b_i\partial_i a_j\right)\partial_j f.
\]
The second-derivative terms cancel because $\partial_i\partial_j f=\partial_j\partial_i f$. Hence this operator is $L_c$, where $c_j=\sum_i(a_i\partial_i b_j-b_i\partial_i a_j)$.

\prob{10.4/2}{Linearity, skew symmetry, and Jacobi}{124}
Linearity and skew symmetry follow immediately from $[A,B]=AB-BA$ applied to $A=L_a$, $B=L_b$. In any associative operator algebra,
\[
 [[A,B],C]=ABC-BAC-CAB+CBA.
\]
Adding its cyclic permutations cancels all six ordered triple products in pairs. Thus the Jacobi identity holds for the operators. Since $v\mapsto L_v$ is injective, all three identities hold for the corresponding vector fields.

\prob{10.4/3}{The cross product is a Lie bracket}{124}
The cross product is bilinear and skew-symmetric. For Jacobi, the vector triple-product identity gives
\[
 (a\times b)\times c=b(a\cdot c)-a(b\cdot c).
\]
Add the two cyclic analogues; symmetry of the dot product cancels every term. Therefore $\R^3$ with its cross product is a Lie algebra.

\prob{10.4/4}{Matrices with the commutator bracket}{125}
Matrix multiplication is bilinear and associative. Therefore $[A,B]=AB-BA$ is bilinear, skew-symmetric, and satisfies Jacobi by the same six-term cancellation in 10.4/2. The space of all $n\times n$ matrices is closed under this operation and is a Lie algebra.

\prob{10.4/5}{Symmetric and skew-symmetric matrices}{125}
For symmetric $A,B$, $[A,B]^T=-[A,B]$, so their commutator is generally not symmetric. For example,
\[
 A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\quad
 B=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad
 [A,B]=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Thus symmetric matrices do not form a Lie algebra under this bracket for $n\ge2$ (the $n=1$ case is abelian). If $A^T=-A$ and $B^T=-B$, then again $[A,B]^T=-[A,B]$, now proving closure. Skew-symmetric matrices form the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{so}(n)$.

\prob{10.4/6}{Coordinate components of the bracket}{125}
Apply the commutator to the coordinate function $x_j$. Since $L_bx_j=b_j$ and $L_ax_j=a_j$,
\[
 [a,b]_j=L_ab_j-L_ba_j
 =\sum_i\left(a_i\frac{\partial b_j}{\partial x_i}-b_i\frac{\partial a_j}{\partial x_i}\right).
\]
This also checks the sign convention used in the other bracket exercises.

\prob{10.4/7}{Commuting flows and vanishing brackets}{125}
Suppose the flows $g^t$ of $a$ and $h^s$ of $b$ commute. Differentiate $g^t(h^s(x))=h^s(g^t(x))$ in $s$ at zero to obtain $Dg^t(x)b(x)=b(g^t(x))$. Differentiating in $t$ at zero yields $Da\,b=Db\,a$, or $[a,b]=0$.

Conversely assume $Db\,a=Da\,b$. Along $g^t(x)$, the two vectors $Dg^t(x)b(x)$ and $b(g^t(x))$ solve the same linear equation $\dot w=Da(g^t(x))w$ with the same initial value. Hence they agree. It follows that $s\mapsto g^t(h^s(x))$ is a solution of $\dot z=b(z)$ starting at $g^t(x)$, so uniqueness gives $g^th^s(x)=h^sg^t(x)$. This is a local statement where both compositions are defined; for complete fields it holds for all real $s,t$.

\prob{10.4/8}{The sign of the rotation-field bracket}{125}
With the usual angular-velocity convention, put $r=x-o$ and $a_\omega(x)=\omega\times r$. Using the bracket defined in 10.4/6,
\[
 [a_\alpha,a_\beta](x)
 =\beta\times(\alpha\times r)-\alpha\times(\beta\times r)
 =-(\alpha\times\beta)\times r
 =-a_{\alpha\times\beta}(x).
\]
\review{The printed answer has the opposite sign. With $L_{[a,b]}=L_aL_b-L_bL_a$ and velocity $a_\omega=\omega\times r$, the minus sign above is required. A direct check uses $\alpha=e_1$, $\beta=e_2$: the bracket at $r=e_1$ equals $-e_2$. The printed plus sign corresponds instead to defining the rotation field as $r\times\omega$, or to reversing the bracket convention.}

\prob{10.5/1}{First integrals near a limit cycle}{125}
For an isolated planar periodic orbit, choose a small transverse segment and its increasing Poincar\'e return map. The fixed point representing the cycle is isolated, so on each side sufficiently close to it, the displacement has a fixed sign. Iterating the map in forward or backward time makes points on that side approach the fixed point. Flowing the segment gives a small annular neighborhood whose trajectories approach the cycle in at least one time direction.

A continuous first integral is constant on the cycle, say with value $c$. It is constant on every nearby trajectory; taking a sequence of points of that trajectory tending to the cycle proves its value is also $c$. Thus it is constant throughout that neighborhood. This includes a semistable planar cycle, using the appropriate time direction separately on each side.
\review{The planar limit-cycle setting is essential. An arbitrary isolated periodic orbit in higher dimension may have transverse saddle directions and a nonconstant first integral: $\dot\theta=1$, $\dot u=u$, $\dot v=-v$ on $S^1\times\R^2$ has the isolated periodic orbit $u=v=0$ and integral $uv$.}

\prob{10.5/2}{Global first integrals of a diagonal linear system}{126}
For $\dot x=x$, $\dot y=ky$, if $k>0$, every trajectory tends to $(0,0)$ as $t\to-\infty$. Continuity then forces any global first integral to equal its value at the origin. For $k=0$, $y$ itself is a nonconstant integral.

For $k<0$, put $a=-k>0$. In the first quadrant $q=x^ay$ is invariant. Define on the whole plane
\[
 f(x,y)=\begin{cases}\exp(-1/(x^ay)),&x>0,\ y>0,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}
\]
This is a nonconstant $C^\infty$ first integral. To check smoothness across the axes, each derivative inside the quadrant is a finite sum of powers of $x,y$ times $e^{-1/(x^ay)}$; on a bounded neighborhood, the exponential dominates every inverse power as either coordinate tends to zero. All derivatives therefore extend by zero, including at the origin. Thus precisely $k\le0$ admit nonconstant global smooth first integrals.

\prob{10.5/3}{The algebra of first integrals}{126}
If $L_vf=L_vg=0$, then $L_v(f+g)=0$ and $L_v(fg)=fL_vg+gL_vf=0$. Constants are also first integrals, and scalar multiples remain first integrals. Therefore these functions form a unital $\R$-algebra (and, where defined, any smooth function of finitely many first integrals is again a first integral).

\prob{10.6/1}{Why the shape of the domain matters}{127}
Take $U=\R^2\setminus\{(0,y):y\ge0\}$ and the field $\partial_x$. This slit plane is connected. Define $f(x,y)=e^{-1/y}$ on $x>0,y>0$, and $f=0$ elsewhere in $U$. The function is smooth because it is flat as $y\downarrow0$, and $\partial_xf=0$ everywhere in $U$. Yet $f(1,1)=e^{-1}$ and $f(-1,1)=0$. It cannot be a function of $y$ alone: horizontal slices have two components above the slit.

\prob{10.7/1}{Kepler's sectorial velocity}{128}
For planar motion let $r$ denote distance and $\varphi$ the polar angle. The determinant $\ell=x\dot y-y\dot x=r^2\dot\varphi$ satisfies
\[
 \dot\ell=x\ddot y-y\ddot x
 =x(-y/r^3)-y(-x/r^3)=0.
\]
Thus $r^2\dot\varphi$ is a first integral wherever the equation is defined. Geometric swept area per unit time is $\ell/2$.

\prob{10.7/2}{Any central force preserves sectorial velocity}{128}
If $\ddot{\boldsymbol r}=a(r)\boldsymbol r$, then
$\frac d{dt}\det(\boldsymbol r,\dot{\boldsymbol r})
=\det(\dot{\boldsymbol r},\dot{\boldsymbol r})+a(r)\det(\boldsymbol r,\boldsymbol r)=0$.
Hence the same integral $r^2\dot\varphi$ exists, independently of the radial force law.

\prob{10.7/3}{Three-dimensional angular momentum}{128}
For a central force,
\[
 \frac d{dt}(\boldsymbol r\times\dot{\boldsymbol r})
 =\dot{\boldsymbol r}\times\dot{\boldsymbol r}
  +\boldsymbol r\times a(r)\boldsymbol r=0.
\]
Every component is therefore a first integral. For unit mass this vector is the angular momentum; a nonzero value also confines the motion to its perpendicular plane.

\prob{10.7/4}{A cyclic coordinate}{128}
Hamilton's equation is $\dot p_i=-\partial H/\partial q_i$. If $H$ is independent of $q_i$, this derivative vanishes identically, so $p_i$ is constant along every solution and is a first integral.

\prob{10.7/5}{A complete equation has global time-dependent integrals}{128}
Fix the reference time $0$ and write $G(s,t)$ for the evolution from $t$ to $s$. Completeness makes
\[
 a(t,x)=G(0,t)x
\]
defined everywhere on the extended phase space. Its components are first integrals: by the evolution law, $a(t,G(t,0)a_0)=a_0$. For fixed $t$ the map $x\mapsto a(t,x)$ is a diffeomorphism, with inverse $G(t,0)$, so its $n$ components are functionally independent even with respect to $x$ alone. Finally any time-dependent first integral $F$ satisfies
\[
 F(t,x)=F(0,a(t,x)).
\]
Thus every such integral is a function of these $n$ integrals. This uses the Euclidean phase coordinates in the problem; on a general manifold the initial-point map is globally manifold-valued and need not admit one global coordinate system.

\Needspace{14\baselineskip}
\section{First-order partial differential equations (\texorpdfstring{$\S11$}{Section 11})}
\prob{11.1/1}{Characteristics of a linear PDE}{129}
Write $u_x-yu_y=0$. The characteristic field is $(1,-y)$, so its equations are $\dot x=1$, $\dot y=-y$. Eliminating the parameter gives $y=Ce^{-x}$, including the characteristic $y=0$.

\prob{11.1/2}{The general solution along these characteristics}{130}
The coordinate $c=ye^x$ is constant on each characteristic, and $(x,y)\mapsto(x,c)$ is a global diffeomorphism. In these coordinates the equation is $u_x|_c=0$, hence
\[
 u(x,y)=F(ye^x)
\]
for an arbitrary differentiable $F$. On the whole plane this is the complete family; on a general restricted domain one must also account for disconnected characteristic segments.

\prob{11.1/3}{Rotational characteristics}{130}
The equation $yu_x=xu_y$ is $L_{(y,-x)}u=0$. Its nonzero characteristics are the circles centered at the origin. Therefore every solution on $\R^2$ is radial:
\[
 u(x,y)=F(x^2+y^2).
\]
For smooth solutions $F$ is smooth on $[0,\infty)$ in the one-sided sense and can be extended smoothly across zero. This follows by applying the even-function Taylor expansion to $u(r,0)$ at $r=0$; away from zero use $F(s)=u(\sqrt s,0)$. Conversely any such $F$ gives a smooth solution. For only $C^1$ solutions, require the composite to be $C^1$ rather than unnecessarily requiring $F$ to be $C^1$ at zero.

\prob{11.1/4}{One invariant need not separate all global characteristics}{130}
For $xu_x=yu_y$, the field is $(x,-y)$ and $xy$ is invariant, but a level $xy=c>0$ has two different branches. The smooth function
\[
 u(x,y)=\begin{cases}e^{-1/(xy)},&x>0,\ y>0,\\0,&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}
\]
satisfies the PDE, with smoothness across the axes following from exponential flatness. Yet $u(1,1)=e^{-1}$ and $u(-1,-1)=0$, despite equal products. Hence not every global solution is a single function of $xy$.

\prob{11.2/1}{Sinusoidal initial data on a transversal}{131}
Every characteristic $ye^x=c$ meets $x=0$ at $(0,c)$. Transporting the initial value $\sin c$ gives $u(x,y)=\sin(ye^x)$. This is the unique global solution since every characteristic meets the initial line exactly once.

\prob{11.2/2}{Noncharacteristic points of a vertical line}{131}
For $yu_x=xu_y$, the characteristic vector at $(1,y)$ is $(y,-1)$. It is transverse to the vertical line $x=1$ exactly when its horizontal component $y$ is nonzero. Thus the only characteristic point of this line is $(1,0)$.

\prob{11.2/3}{A globally nonunique Cauchy problem}{131}
The solution must be $u=F(x^2+y^2)$, and its restriction to $x=1$ gives $F(1+y^2)=y^2$. Thus $F(s)=s-1$ for $s\ge1$, with no values specified for $0\le s<1$ except smooth matching. One solution is $u=x^2+y^2-1$. Infinitely many others are
\[
 u=x^2+y^2-1+B(x^2+y^2),
\]
where $B$ is any smooth nonzero bump supported in $(0,1)$. Existence holds, but global uniqueness fails because the initial line misses all circles of radius less than one.

\prob{11.3/1}{An inhomogeneous transport equation}{132}
For $u_x-yu_y=y$ and $u(0,y)=\sin y$, use the characteristic $y=ce^{-x}$. Along it, $du/dx=ce^{-x}$, giving $u=\sin c+c(1-e^{-x})$. Substituting $c=ye^x$ yields
\[
 \boxed{u(x,y)=\sin(ye^x)+y(e^x-1)}.
\]
Direct differentiation verifies both the PDE and the data.

\prob{11.4/1}{Burgers evolution of arctangent data}{133}
For the printed data $u(0,x)=\arctan x$ in $u_t+uu_x=0$, label a particle by its initial coordinate $a$. Characteristics give
\[
 x=a+t\arctan a,\qquad u=\arctan a.
\]
Equivalently the graph at time $t$ is $x=\tan u+tu$, $-\pi/2<u<\pi/2$. Its projection derivative is
\[
 \frac{\partial x}{\partial a}=1+\frac{t}{1+a^2},\qquad
 u_x=\frac1{1+a^2+t}.
\]
For every $t>-1$ the map $a\mapsto x$ is an increasing diffeomorphism of $\R$. Thus the classical solution exists for all forward time, with progressively flatter increasing graphs. At $t=-1$ its slope blows up at $a=0$; for $t<-1$ the characteristic surface folds.
\review{The decreasing graph and positive breaking time $\pi/2$ printed with this problem are inconsistent with the displayed initial condition $\arctan x$. The formula above solves the stated data. A decreasing profile instead breaks forward in time at $t_*=-1/\min u_0'$ when that minimum is negative; even the unscaled $\operatorname{arccot}x$ would give $t_*=1$, not $\pi/2$.}

\prob{11.4/2}{A velocity field in an external force}{133}
If a particle follows $\dot x=u(t,x)$ and has acceleration $F(x)$, the chain rule gives $\ddot x=u_t+u_x\dot x=u_t+uu_x$. Therefore the Eulerian velocity equation is $u_t+uu_x=F(x)$ (unit mass, or $F$ interpreted as force per unit mass).

\prob{11.4/3}{Harmonic focusing}{133}
For $F(x)=-x$ with zero initial velocity, a particle starting at $a$ has $x=a\cos t$, $u=-a\sin t$. While $\cos t\ne0$, eliminate $a$ to obtain $u(t,x)=-x\tan t$. The maximal time strip containing $t=0$ is $|t|<\pi/2$. At its endpoints all particle positions focus at zero and no single smooth velocity field represents the family.

\prob{11.4/4}{The first breakdown time for sinusoidal forcing}{133}
Let $X(t,a)$ solve $X''=\sin X$, $X(0,a)=a$, $X_t(0,a)=0$. Then $u(t,X(t,a))=X_t(t,a)$ as long as $J=X_a$ stays positive. The variational equation is
\[
 J''=(\cos X)J,\quad J(0)=1,\ J'(0)=0.
\]
Before its first zero and for $0\le t<\pi/2$, variation of constants yields
\[
 J(t)=\cos t+\int_0^t\sin(t-s)(1+\cos X(s,a))J(s)\dd s\ge\cos t>0.
\]
A first-zero argument therefore shows no zero occurs before $\pi/2$. Also $|X(t,a)-a|\le t^2/2$, so the increasing map $a\mapsto X(t,a)$ is onto, giving a global smooth velocity field on each such strip.

For $a=\pi$, the particle is stationary, and $J=\cos t$, $J_t=-\sin t$. Hence $u_x(t,\pi)=J_t/J=-\tan t$ diverges as $t\uparrow\pi/2$. The largest width is consequently $C=\pi/2$.

\prob{11.5/1}{Characteristics in the extended space}{134}
The characteristic vector for $u_t+uu_x=0$ in $(t,x,u)$-space is $(1,u,0)$. Integrating gives $(t,x,u)=(s,x_0+u_0s,u_0)$ after choosing the initial time as zero. These are straight lines; their projections to $(t,x)$ are the particle trajectories.

\prob{11.5/2}{A local normal form for a quasilinear equation}{135}
For $\sum a_i(x,u)u_{x_i}=b(x,u)$, the characteristic vector is $A=(a,b)$. If $a\ne0$, relabel coordinates so $a_1\ne0$. Use the hypersurface $x_1=x_1^0$ as a transversal and label points on it by $(x_2^0,\ldots,x_n^0,u^0)$. Following the local characteristic flow defines smooth coordinates $(s,x_2^0,\ldots,x_n^0,u^0)$ by the inverse function theorem. In these coordinates $A=\partial_s$ and integral hypersurfaces that are graphs take the form $u^0=U(s,x_2^0,\ldots,x_n^0)$ with $U_s=0$.

For a solution graph through the reference point, its intersection with the transversal is a graph in $(x_2^0,\ldots,x_n^0,u^0)$; flowing it gives the required representation locally. The proviso about graphs is necessary for a change of coordinates mixing dependent and independent variables.

\prob{11.6/1}{Local existence and uniqueness for noncharacteristic data}{136}
Parametrize the initial hypersurface by $x=\gamma(z)$, $z\in\R^{n-1}$, and prescribe $u=\phi(z)$. Solve the characteristic system $X_s=a(X,U)$, $U_s=b(X,U)$ with $(X,U)(0,z)=(\gamma(z),\phi(z))$. The derivative of $(s,z)\mapsto X(s,z)$ at the initial point has columns $a$ and the tangent vectors $\partial_{z_j}\gamma$. Noncharacteristicity says these columns form a basis. Thus this map is locally invertible, and $u(x)=U(s(x),z(x))$ is smooth. Its graph is tangent to $(a,b)$, so it solves the PDE and the data. Any other solution with the same data contains the same characteristic segments by ODE uniqueness, and hence gives the same graph locally.

\prob{11.7/1}{The characteristic system preserves the equation surface}{136}
For $F(x,p,y)=0$, the characteristic system is
\[
 \dot x=F_p,\quad \dot p=-F_x-pF_y,\quad \dot y=p\cdot F_p.
\]
The chain rule gives $\dot F=F_x\cdot F_p+F_p\cdot(-F_x-pF_y)+F_y(p\cdot F_p)=0$. Thus a characteristic starting on $E=\{F=0\}$ remains on $E$ throughout its interval of existence.

\prob{11.7/2}{Solution jets and characteristics}{137}
Let $u$ be a $C^2$ solution and consider its first-jet graph $j^1u=(x,Du(x),u(x))$. Differentiating $F(x,Du,u)=0$ gives
\[
 F_x+D^2u\,F_p+(Du)F_y=0.
\]
The tangent vector to $j^1u$ above $\dot x=F_p$ is therefore
$(F_p,D^2u\,F_p,Du\cdot F_p)=(F_p,-F_x-pF_y,p\cdot F_p)$.
The characteristic field is tangent to the jet graph, so uniqueness makes its short trajectories stay in that graph. Conversely, if the jet graph is made of characteristics of the equation, these characteristics lie in $E$ by definition, so $F(x,Du,u)=0$ pointwise.
\review{Tangency to the displayed vector field alone, without membership in $E$, is not enough: it would only constrain which level of $F$ the jet graph occupies. The phrase ``characteristics of the equation'' includes the condition $F=0$.}

\prob{11.7/3}{Projection to quasilinear characteristics}{137}
Write a quasilinear equation as $F(x,p,y)=a(x,y)\cdot p-b(x,y)=0$. Then $\dot x=F_p=a(x,y)$ and, on $E$, $\dot y=p\cdot F_p=a\cdot p=b$. The projection to $(x,y)$ is exactly the characteristic system $(\dot x,\dot y)=(a,b)$ of the quasilinear equation.

\prob{11.7/4*}{Coordinate invariance of characteristics}{137}
Let $\alpha=dy-\sum_i p_i\,dx_i$ be the contact form. Its restriction to each contact plane $C=\ker\alpha$ has the nondegenerate skew form $d\alpha=\sum_i dx_i\wedge dp_i$. On $E=\{F=0\}$, set $K=TE\cap C$. Since $F_p\ne0$, $K$ is a hyperplane in the symplectic vector space $C$. The kernel of $d\alpha|_K$ is a one-dimensional line and is intrinsic to $E$ and the contact planes.

The displayed characteristic vector $X_F$ lies in $K$: $\alpha(X_F)=0$ and $dF(X_F)=0$. For any $Z\in K$,
\[
 d\alpha(X_F,Z)=F_p\cdot Z_p+(F_x+pF_y)\cdot Z_x=dF(Z)=0,
\]
where $Z_y=p\cdot Z_x$ was used. Thus $X_F$ spans this intrinsic line.

A change $(x,y)\mapsto(X,Y)$ lifts to jet coordinates wherever a transformed graph remains a graph, defining $P$ by $dY-P\cdot dX=\lambda(dy-p\cdot dx)$ with $\lambda\ne0$. It carries contact planes to contact planes, and on them the exterior derivatives differ only by the nonzero factor $\lambda$. It therefore carries the kernel line above to the corresponding kernel line on the transformed equation surface. Its unparametrized characteristic curves are preserved. Finally replacing $F$ by $hF$, $h\ne0$, changes $X_F$ on $E$ to $hX_F$, so it changes speed but not characteristics. This proves both requested invariances, and indeed the contact-transformation version as well.

\prob{11.7/5}{Distance to a smooth plane curve}{137}
Near a point of a smooth embedded curve use tubular coordinates $x=\gamma(s)+r n(s)$, with $s$ arclength and $n$ the unit normal. In a sufficiently small tube the nearest point is $\gamma(s)$ and the distance is $u=|r|$. Since $n\cdot\partial_s x=0$ and $n\cdot\partial_r x=1$, one has $\nabla r=n$. Off the curve, $\nabla u=\operatorname{sgn}(r)n$, so $u_{x_1}^2+u_{x_2}^2=1$. The unsigned distance is not differentiable on the curve itself, which is why it is excluded.

\prob{11.7/6}{Distance to a smooth submanifold}{137--138}
In a tubular neighborhood where the nearest-point projection $\pi(x)$ to the embedded submanifold is unique and smooth, write $\nu=x-\pi(x)$, $u=|\nu|>0$. The vector $\nu$ is perpendicular to the tangent space containing $D\pi(x)h$. Therefore
\[
 Du(x)h=\frac{\nu\cdot(h-D\pi(x)h)}{|\nu|}=\frac{\nu\cdot h}{|\nu|}.
\]
It follows that $\nabla u=\nu/|\nu|$ and $|\nabla u|^2=1$. This is a local tubular-neighborhood assertion, excluding the submanifold and any cut locus; a uniform tube need not exist for a noncompact submanifold.

\prob{11.7/7}{Every smooth eikonal solution is locally a distance plus a constant}{138}
Suppose $|\nabla u|=1$. Differentiation gives $D^2u\,\nabla u=0$. Along an integral curve of $\nabla u$, the gradient is consequently constant, so the curve is a straight unit-speed line, and $u$ increases along it at rate one. A nearby regular level hypersurface $S=\{u=c\}$ is orthogonal to these lines. The tubular-neighborhood theorem then identifies their parameter with signed distance from $S$.

To obtain the literal unsigned distance on a whole neighborhood of the chosen point $x_0$, choose $c<u(x_0)$ sufficiently close and restrict the neighborhood to the side $u>c$. There $u(x)=c+\operatorname{dist}(x,S)$. Choosing $S$ through $x_0$ instead would give signed distance and would not equal unsigned distance on both sides.

\prob{11.7/8}{Hamilton--Jacobi characteristics}{138}
If $F=H(x,p)$ is independent of $y$, the characteristic equations reduce to $\dot x=H_p$, $\dot p=-H_x$, $\dot y=p\cdot H_p$. Their $(x,p)$ projections are precisely Hamiltonian trajectories, and 11.7/1 ensures they remain on $H=0$. Conversely any such Hamiltonian trajectory lifts by integrating $\dot y=p\cdot\dot x$ with an arbitrary initial value of $y$.

\Needspace{14\baselineskip}
\section{Conservative systems with one degree of freedom (\texorpdfstring{$\S12$}{Section 12})}
Throughout this section write $y=\dot x$ and $H(x,y)=y^2/2+U(x)$. A level is drawn by taking both graphs $y=\pm\sqrt{2(E-U(x))}$ over $\{U\le E\}$. Its upper half moves right and its lower half moves left. A noncritical turning point joins these halves smoothly; an equilibrium is a separate orbit even when it belongs to a separatrix level. The drawings following the solutions implement this rule.

\prob{12.3/1}{Pendulum, center, and saddle energy levels}{142}
For the pendulum, $U=-\cos x$ and $y^2=2(E+\cos x)$. There are no levels for $E<-1$. At $E=-1$ there are the centers $(2k\pi,0)$. For $-1<E<1$, each potential well contains a closed oval. At $E=1$ the level has the saddles $((2k+1)\pi,0)$ and the connecting separatrix arcs $y=\pm2|\cos(x/2)|$. For $E>1$ the upper and lower graphs extend across the whole real axis without turning. On the cylinder $x\bmod2\pi$ these are periodic rotations; on the plane their lifts are not closed.

For $\ddot x=-x$, the levels are circles $x^2+y^2=2E$ (or the point zero when $E=0$). For $\ddot x=x$, they are hyperbolas $y^2-x^2=2E$. At $E=0$ the two lines $y=\pm x$ consist of the equilibrium and four separate separatrix rays. Figure~\ref{fig:c2basic} sketches all three cases.

\prob{12.3/2}{Kepler levels and the four potential profiles}{142}
For the radial Kepler potential $U=-1/x+C/x^2$ take the physical domain $x>0$ and $C>0$. Its unique minimum is at $x=2C$ with value $-1/(4C)$; $U\to+\infty$ as $x\downarrow0$ and $U\to0^-$ as $x\to\infty$. Thus:
\begin{itemize}
\item Below $-1/(4C)$ the level is empty; at that value it is the equilibrium.
\item For $-1/(4C)<E<0$, it is a closed oval between two positive turning points, the roots of $Ex^2+x-C=0$.
\item For $E=0$, it has one turning point $x=C$, and two branches tending to $y=0$ at infinity, joined at that turning point.
\item For $E>0$, it has one positive turning point and branches tending to $y=\pm\sqrt{2E}$ at infinity.
\end{itemize}
The exact equation is $y^2=2E+2/x-2C/x^2$. If $C=0$, $U=-1/x$ is monotone: levels with $E<0$ turn once and run into the collision boundary $x=0$; nonnegative levels have no finite turning point. For $C<0$, the potential is likewise strictly increasing from $-\infty$ to $0$ and has the same qualitative alternatives, with a stronger collision singularity.

For the four schematic profiles of Figure 96, the corresponding sketches are in Figure~\ref{fig:c2profiles}. In profile I, a center and a saddle bound one well; the saddle level has a homoclinic loop on the well side and escape branches on the other side. Profile II also has one saddle and one center, but the finite-height tails change which branches escape as the energy passes a tail height. Profile III has, in order, a center, a lower saddle, a second center, and a higher saddle. Crossing the lower saddle energy joins the two wells; crossing the higher one opens escape to the right. Profile IV has two centers separated by one saddle; its unequal tail heights control which outer branches escape. For each profile the full answer at any specified energy is obtained by the two square-root graphs above every allowed interval. The source specifies shapes rather than formulas, so the plotted numerical heights and horizontal scales are schematic, not additional data attributed to the book.

\prob{12.4/1}{Tangents to saddle separatrices}{144}
At a nondegenerate maximum $\xi$, expand
\[
 U(x)=U(\xi)+\tfrac12U''(\xi)(x-\xi)^2+o((x-\xi)^2).
\]
On the separatrix level $E=U(\xi)$ this gives $y^2=-U''(\xi)(x-\xi)^2+o((x-\xi)^2)$. Therefore the two tangent lines are $y=\pm\sqrt{-U''(\xi)}(x-\xi)$. They are also the stable and unstable eigendirections of the linearized system.

\prob{12.5/1}{Completeness for positive many-body potential energy}{145}
For $m_i\ddot x_i=-\partial_iU$, $m_i>0$, on all of $\R^N$, energy conservation gives
\[
 E=\sum_i\frac{m_i\dot x_i^2}{2}+U(x),\qquad
 |\dot x_i|\le\sqrt{2E/m_i}
\]
when $U>0$. Hence on every finite time interval each coordinate and velocity stays bounded. The phase point lies in a compact subset of the smooth equation's full phase space, so the extension theorem excludes a finite maximal endpoint. Every solution is complete. A lower bound $U\ge B$ suffices by replacing $E$ with $E-B$; no upper bound on $U$ or its derivatives is required.

\prob{12.9/1}{Time graphs near the pendulum separatrix}{149}
Let $E=1-\delta$, $0<\delta\ll1$. The turning angle $A$ obeys $\cos A=-E$, so $A=\pi-\sqrt{2\delta}+O(\delta^{3/2})$. Starting at $x=0$ with positive velocity, the pendulum crosses the bottom rapidly, then spends a long time near $A$, returns rapidly through zero, and waits near $-A$. The angle graph has long rounded plateaus near $\pm A$, while $y(t)$ has alternating narrow positive and negative pulses, vanishing at the turning points. The maximum speed is $\sqrt{2(E+1)}\to2$.

The limiting positive separatrix passage is exactly
\[
 x_s(t)=4\arctan(e^t)-\pi,\qquad y_s(t)=2\operatorname{sech}t.
\]
Its negative counterpart describes the return passage. Finite-energy oscillations concatenate well-separated approximations to these passages; Figure~\ref{fig:c2time} shows numerical quadrature of a near-critical periodic motion.

\prob{12.9/2}{The logarithmic divergence of the pendulum period}{149}
Write $k=\sin(A/2)=\sqrt{(E+1)/2}$. Substituting $\sin(x/2)=k\sin\phi$ into the period quadrature gives
\[
 T(E)=4\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{d\phi}{\sqrt{1-k^2\sin^2\phi}}.
\]
Set $\eta=\sqrt{1-k^2}=\sqrt{(1-E)/2}$. Only the endpoint $\phi=\pi/2$ is singular. With $s=\pi/2-\phi$, its denominator is $\sqrt{\eta^2+(1-\eta^2)\sin^2s}$. On a fixed small interval, replacing $\sin s$ by $s$ changes the integral by a bounded amount uniformly in $\eta$; this follows from $\sin s=s+O(s^3)$. The model integral is $\operatorname{arsinh}(c/\eta)=\log(1/\eta)+O(1)$. The remainder away from the endpoint stays bounded. Consequently
\[
 \boxed{T(E)=2\log\frac1{1-E}+O(1)},\qquad E\uparrow1.
\]
Thus the divergence is logarithmic, with positive sign. More precise evaluation gives $T(E)=2\log(32/(1-E))+o(1)$, but the coefficient and bounded remainder already answer the problem. The period is not proportional to a positive multiple of $\log(1-E)$, which tends to minus infinity.

\prob{12.9/3}{Six oscillatory potentials}{149}
For each sign take $y^2=2(E-U(x))$; Figures~\ref{fig:c2potplus}--\ref{fig:c2potminus} show both signs. Minima of $U$ are centers, nondegenerate maxima are saddles, and the corresponding critical energy levels are their separatrices.
\begin{enumerate}
\item $U=x\sin x$ is even, with a minimum at zero ($U''(0)=2$). The remaining critical points solve $\sin x+x\cos x=0$, or $\tan x=-x$. The alternating wells and barriers grow in height in absolute value. For any fixed finite energy there are distant forbidden barriers, so all allowed components are bounded, although there are infinitely many distant wells. The negative potential reverses centers and saddles and the barrier ordering.
\item $U=\sin x/x$, defined as $1$ at zero, is even and tends to zero. Zero is a maximum, since $U=1-x^2/6+O(x^4)$. The other extrema solve $x\cos x-\sin x=0$, or $\tan x=x$, with decaying heights. For $E>0$, all sufficiently distant points are allowed; for $E<0$, only finitely many wells are accessible. At $E=0$ there are infinitely many alternating allowed and forbidden intervals. Negating $U$ interchanges maxima and minima and changes which intervals are allowed. These statements concern accessibility; the square-root rule determines the exact branches.
\item $U=\sin(x^2)$ is even and lies between $-1$ and $1$. Zero is a minimum. The other critical points satisfy $x^2=\pi/2+k\pi$, $k\ge0$, and alternate maxima of height $1$ and minima of height $-1$. For $-1<E<1$, allowed intervals give closed ovals; the central component is present only for $E\ge0$, with a singleton at $E=0$. At $E=1$ all maxima lie on the separatrix level. For $E>1$ there are two graphs over the entire line. The wells become narrower at large $|x|$. For the negative potential, zero becomes a maximum of height zero, and the roles of the other extrema reverse.
\end{enumerate}
The exact energy equations, together with the rule at the start of this section, specify every level, including empty levels and equilibrium singletons not individually visible at the scale of a sketch.

\prob{12.9/4}{Six oscillatory force laws}{149}
Integrate $U'=-F$, taking an irrelevant additive constant to be zero. For the plus force in each pair,
\[
 \begin{array}{c|c}
 F(x)&U(x)\\\hline
 x\sin x&x\cos x-\sin x\\
 \sin x/x&-\displaystyle\int_0^x\frac{\sin s}{s}\dd s\\
 \sin(x^2)&-\displaystyle\int_0^x\sin(s^2)\dd s
 \end{array}
\]
Use the continuous value $F(0)=1$ in the middle row. Negating the force negates the potential. The energy levels again follow from $y^2=2(E-U(x))$; Figures~\ref{fig:c2forceplus}--\ref{fig:c2forceminus} show representative levels for all six cases.

For a simple zero $\xi$ of $F$, the equilibrium is a center if $F'(\xi)<0$ and a saddle if $F'(\xi)>0$. This gives a precise classification for the sketches:
\begin{itemize}
\item For $F=x\sin x$, the nonzero zeros are $\xi=k\pi$, and $F'(\xi)=k\pi(-1)^k$. At zero, $F=x^2+O(x^4)$ and $U=-x^3/3+O(x^5)$, so this is a degenerate equilibrium rather than a center or ordinary saddle.
\item For $F=\sin x/x$, the zeros are $k\pi$, $k\ne0$, and $F'(k\pi)=(-1)^k/(k\pi)$. Zero is not an equilibrium. The potential is bounded and approaches finite, generally different, limits at the two ends of the line; energies above its global maximum give two through-going branches.
\item For $F=\sin(x^2)$, the nonzero zeros are $\xi=\pm\sqrt{k\pi}$, $k\ge1$, with $F'(\xi)=2\xi(-1)^k$. At zero, again $F=x^2+O(x^6)$ and $U=-x^3/3+O(x^7)$, giving a degenerate equilibrium. Its potential also approaches finite limits at infinity.
\end{itemize}
For each negative force, reverse the signs in this test. In particular the two signs exchange centers and saddles at every simple zero. At the degenerate origin the zero-energy level has a cusp with two branches on one side and the origin as a separate orbit; negating the force reflects which side is accessible.

\prob{12.10/1}{Energy drift and cycles under a small perturbation}{149--151}
Consider $\dot x=y+\varepsilon f_1(x,y)$, $\dot y=-x+\varepsilon f_2(x,y)$. On a fixed annulus $0<a\le\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\le b<R$, small $\varepsilon$ preserves rotation and permits a smooth first-return map. With $H=(x^2+y^2)/2$,
\[
 \dot H=\varepsilon(xf_1+yf_2).
\]
A return takes time $2\pi+O(\varepsilon)$ and its trajectory differs by $O(\varepsilon)$ from $(A\cos t,-A\sin t)$. Therefore
\[
 \Delta H=\varepsilon\mathcal F(A)+O(\varepsilon^2),\quad
 \mathcal F(A)=\int_0^{2\pi}(xf_1+yf_2)(A\cos t,-A\sin t)\dd t
 =\oint_{\text{counterclockwise}}(f_1\,dy-f_2\,dx).
\]
The last orientation is important: the unperturbed motion itself is clockwise. For $\varepsilon>0$, positive $\mathcal F$ gives outward drift and negative $\mathcal F$ inward drift, wherever the leading term is bounded away from zero. A simple positive root $A_0$ yields a unique nearby periodic orbit by applying the implicit function theorem to the return displacement divided by $\varepsilon$. Its radius on the transversal is $A_0+O(\varepsilon)$. Since
\[
 P_\varepsilon(A)=A+\varepsilon\frac{\mathcal F(A)}A+O(\varepsilon^2),
\]
this cycle is attracting if $\varepsilon\mathcal F'(A_0)<0$ and repelling if it is positive. A multiple root needs higher-order analysis, and behavior arbitrarily near the origin needs a separate equilibrium analysis.

For the Van der Pol example, $f_1=0$, $f_2=y(1-x^2)$, so
\[
 \mathcal F(A)=A^2\int_0^{2\pi}\sin^2t\dd t
 -A^4\int_0^{2\pi}\sin^2t\cos^2t\dd t
 =\pi(A^2-A^4/4).
\]
Its simple positive root is $A_0=2$, and $\mathcal F'(2)=-4\pi$. Thus small positive $\varepsilon$ produces an attracting limit cycle near the circle of radius two, provided the domain contains that circle and a neighborhood. For negative $\varepsilon$ the stability reverses.

\prob{12.10/2*}{Sustained rotations of a pendulum with weak friction and torque}{151}
Write the equation on the cylinder as
\[
 \dot x=y,\qquad \dot y=M-\sin x-\varepsilon y,\qquad \varepsilon>0.
\]
Changing $(x,y,M)$ to $(-x,-y,-M)$ reverses the torque, so it suffices to study $M\ge0$. We give the small-friction regimes, an exact shooting characterization of the transition, and the leading transition formula. A rotation is a periodic orbit on the cylinder, not a periodic angle on its real-line cover.

\paragraph{Resting states and the absence of periodic librations.}
For $0\le M<1$, equilibria occur at $x_c=\arcsin M$ and $x_s=\pi-\arcsin M$ modulo $2\pi$, with $y=0$. The eigenvalues obey $\lambda^2+\varepsilon\lambda+\cos x_*=0$. Thus $x_c$ is an attracting equilibrium (a focus for $\varepsilon^2<4\cos x_c$) and $x_s$ is a saddle. At $M=1$ they merge in a saddle-node; for $M>1$ there is no equilibrium.

On the real-line cover the tilted energy
\[
 W=\tfrac12y^2-\cos x-Mx
\]
satisfies $\dot W=-\varepsilon y^2$. Thus there is no nonconstant periodic motion with zero winding number: integrating over a period would give $\int y^2dt=0$. Any self-sustained periodic motion must rotate. In particular at $M=0$ no rotation can persist either, since ordinary energy strictly decreases off rest.

\paragraph{The weak-torque scale and the rotation balance.}
Set $M=\varepsilon\mu$. For the untilted pendulum energy $H=y^2/2-\cos x$, one has $\dot H=\varepsilon(\mu y-y^2)$. On an unperturbed positive rotation of energy $E>1$, $y=\sqrt{2(E+\cos x)}$. During one revolution,
\[
 \Delta H=\varepsilon\{2\pi\mu-I(E)\}+O(\varepsilon^2),\qquad
 I(E)=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\sqrt{2(E+\cos x)}\dd x.
\]
This expansion is uniform on compact energy intervals strictly above $1$. Here
\[
 I(1)=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}2\cos(x/2)\dd x=8,\quad
 I'(E)=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\frac{dx}{\sqrt{2(E+\cos x)}}>0,
\]
and $I(E)\to\infty$. Hence for each fixed $\mu>4/\pi$ there is exactly one $E_\mu>1$ solving $I(E_\mu)=2\pi\mu$. The return-map implicit function theorem gives a nearby attracting rotation for sufficiently small $\varepsilon$, with energy $E_\mu+O(\varepsilon)$ on a fixed transversal. Its leading period is $I'(E_\mu)$. The restoring sign follows because $2\pi\mu-I(E)$ decreases strictly with $E$.

\paragraph{Separatrix transition and retrapping torque.}
The rotation is born through a saddle connection near the pendulum separatrix, where the preceding regular-return expansion is not uniform. Parametrize the positive unperturbed separatrix by
$x_s(t)=4\arctan e^t-\pi$, $y_s(t)=2\operatorname{sech}t$.
The first-order difference in energy between the unstable and stable saddle branches is
\[
 \varepsilon\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}(\mu y_s-y_s^2)\dd t
 =\varepsilon(2\pi\mu-8).
\]
Indeed $\int y_sdt=2\pi$ and $\int y_s^2dt=8$. Smooth dependence of the saddle manifolds on parameters, measured on a transversal away from the saddle, makes this the first variation of their splitting. Its derivative in $\mu$ is $2\pi\ne0$, so the implicit function theorem gives a transition torque
\[
 \boxed{M_r(\varepsilon)=\frac4\pi\varepsilon+o(\varepsilon)}.
\]
At this torque, the saddle's unstable branch joins its next translate on the cover (a homoclinic loop on the cylinder). The rotation period tends to infinity there. The formula is asymptotic, not an exact threshold for finite damping.

For an exact implicit specification at a chosen small $\varepsilon$, integrate the positive branch of
\[
 y\frac{dy}{dx}=M-\sin x-\varepsilon y
\]
from the outgoing saddle at $x_s$ and compare it on a transverse line with the incoming branch of the saddle at $x_s+2\pi$. The value $M=M_r$ makes the branches agree, with $y\to0$ at both saddles. The local slope at the outgoing endpoint is the positive root of $\lambda^2+\varepsilon\lambda+\cos x_s=0$, so the singular endpoint can be initialized by this slope or by the smooth time-parametrized system.

\paragraph{Why the transition gives the phase portrait.}
Increasing $M$ at fixed $\varepsilon$ increases the right-hand side of the $y(x)$ equation on $y>0$. The outgoing saddle branch moves toward passage over the next barrier rather than return into the well; at equality it is the saddle connection. Above the connection a rotating return orbit exists, whereas below it the outgoing branch is captured by the next well. The same comparison on the positive transverse section gives an interval as the domain of rotating returns. Every fixed point of its return map has multiplier
\[
 P'=\exp\!\left(\int_0^T\operatorname{div}(y,M-\sin x-\varepsilon y)\dd t\right)
 =e^{-\varepsilon T}<1.
\]
Consequently every rotation is attracting, and there can be at most one: two attracting simple fixed points on an interval would require an intervening fixed point where the return displacement crosses in the opposite direction. This also gives the stability without averaging. A negative rotating periodic orbit is impossible for $M>0$, since the exact energy balance over a period would be $-2\pi M=\varepsilon\int y^2dt>0$. Contractible cycles have already been excluded.

For sufficiently small positive friction the resulting regimes are:
\begin{itemize}
\item $0\le M<M_r$: no sustained rotation; apart from saddle trajectories, motions settle into a resting well.
\item $M=M_r$: the saddle connection is the threshold orbit and is not a finite-period oscillation.
\item $M_r<M<1$: an attracting resting state and an attracting rotating cycle coexist. The saddle's stable manifold separates their basins. This is hysteresis: starting from rest and reducing the torque from a rotating state need not produce the same outcome.
\item $M>1$: there is no resting state and a unique attracting positive rotation. At $M=1$ the resting saddle-node remains as a nonhyperbolic exception while the rotating attractor already exists for small friction.
\end{itemize}
For $M>1$, existence can also be seen directly from the trapping horizontal strip $(M-1)/\varepsilon\le y\le(M+1)/\varepsilon$: the vector field points inward and $x$ advances, so a transverse return map has a fixed point. For a fixed $0<M<1$ and $\varepsilon\to0$, the rotating state is likewise well above the threshold and coexists with rest. Its large speed is $y=M/\varepsilon+O(\varepsilon/M)$ and its period is asymptotic to $2\pi\varepsilon/M$. The formulas for $M=\varepsilon\mu$ describe the different, near-threshold scale. Negative torque gives the reflected portrait. No claim about large-friction bifurcations is needed for this small-friction exercise.

All subparts of the numbered exercises are included. The starred problems are 7.1/4, 10.3/2, 11.7/4, and 12.10/2. Figures are original drawings; numerical sampling is used only to illustrate formulas established in the text. The source is self-contained: the drawings are included as TikZ paths and require no separate image files.

\paragraph{Suggested review order.}
Start with 7.1/4--7 (global and time-preserving straightening), 7.3/5 (the valid long-time scale), 8.5/1--3 (implicit equations and envelopes), 9.3/1 (closed subgroups), and 10.3/2 (derivations). Then check 10.4/8 (the bracket sign), 10.5/1 (the planar hypothesis), 11.4/1 (the mismatch between the printed data and illustration), and 11.7/4 (contact invariance). Finish with 12.9/2 (the logarithmic period) and 12.10/2 (the asymptotic, rather than exact, retrapping threshold).

\paragraph{Source.}
Vladimir I. Arnold, \emph{Ordinary Differential Equations}, third edition, translated by Roger Cooke, Springer-Verlag, 1992, Chapter 2, pp.~89--151. Exercise labels and equations were checked against the library scan. These solutions are an independent worked companion and are intended for mathematical review.
